food.text: In the early Viking Age the mouldboard plough revolutionised agriculture in Scandinavia. It made it possible to farm even poor soils, which widened the land available for growing food.

In the cold north, grapes and olives could not be grown, so beer was the commoner's drink while wine was an expensive import. Olive oil was also costly, and oils of poppy, walnut, hazel and filbert were the cheaper alternatives.

Wheat was a luxury in northern Europe and could cost at least twice as much as barley and rye. Barley was the most widely grown grain, but a great percentage of the harvest went into beer, while rye was the principal bread grain.

Grains of rye, barley, oat and wheat dated to the 8th century have been found and examined in Ribe. They are believed to have been cultivated locally, showing that farmers there grew a range of cereals.
Viking-age grains and flour were made into porridges, some cooked with milk and some cooked with fruit and sweetened with honey. They were also baked into various forms of bread.
Remains of bread found mainly at Birka in Sweden were made of barley and wheat. It is unclear whether the Norse leavened their breads, but their ovens and baking utensils suggest that they did.
Kale, a form of cabbage, was especially important in Denmark and Sweden. It kept well and could be harvested after the first frost, when it even tasted better, so it gave fresh food in winter.
Besides weapons, walrus ivory and wax, Viking-age exports included salt and cod. From the 10th century, hunting birds were sometimes sent from Norway to the European aristocracy as an exotic export.

Flax was a very important crop for the Vikings, used for oil extraction, food, and most importantly the production of linen. More than 40% of all known Viking Age textile recoveries can be traced as linen. The real share was probably much higher, since linen is poorly preserved compared to wool.

Flax was a very important Viking crop, used for oil extraction, food and, above all, linen. More than 40% of all known Viking Age textile recoveries are linen, and the real share was probably higher because linen preserves poorly.

art.text: Interlace, in which bands are looped, braided and knotted into complex patterns, is a key feature of the "Style II" animal style decoration of Migration Period art. It is found widely across Northern Europe. Typically the long "ribbons" end in an animal's head.

The Oseberg Ship burial is the most sumptuous Viking funeral discovered so far. It was made for a woman, probably a queen or a priestess, who lived in the 9th century. Grave goods like these symbolized status and also marked key moments or successes in a person's life.
Around AD 965 Harald Bluetooth declared Denmark Christian, and he raised the larger of the two Jelling Stones. Denmark was the first Scandinavian country to Christianize.

By about 700 interlace became less common in most of Europe, but it kept developing in Scandinavia and the British Isles. There it appears on metalwork, woodcarving, runestones, high crosses and illuminated manuscripts from the 7th to the 12th centuries.

Viking kings and chieftains were honoured with tumuli, runestones and other memorials across Scandinavia. Some of the most notable are at the Borre mound cemetery in Norway, at Birka and Gamla Uppsala in Sweden, and at Lindholm Høje and Jelling in Denmark.

The earliest signs of Christianization in Scandinavia came in the 830s, when Ansgar built churches in Birka and Hedeby. These were among the first Christian buildings in a region that had long had pagan temples.

The earliest visual representations of the medieval harp come from Scottish, Pictish, Viking and Norse cultures around the eighth century. Scandinavian groups may have brought the three-sided harp to the continent of Europe and inspired the development of the medieval harp.

Grave goods reflected a person's trade as well as status. An artisan such as a blacksmith could receive his entire set of tools, and women were provided with their jewelry and often with tools for female and household activities.

war.text: The Battle of Svolder was a large naval battle fought in September 1000 in the western Baltic Sea. King Olaf of Norway faced an alliance of the Kings of Denmark and Sweden and Olaf's enemies in Norway. It was tied to Norway's unification and the spread of Christianity in Scandinavia.

Arson was a technique sometimes used in Scandinavian blood feuds and political conflicts to assassinate an opponent. Attackers would pile wood, brush and other combustible material against the outside of a dwelling and set it alight, typically surrounding the house to stop anyone inside from escaping. Women, the elderly and small children were sometimes allowed to leave, which left everyone else to the fire.

Olaf Tryggvason was ambushed by Svein Forkbeard of Denmark, Olof Skötkonung of Sweden and Eirik Hákonarson, Jarl of Lade. According to the Saga of King Olaf I Tryggvason, Olaf had 60 warships plus 11 from the Jomvikings. The sagas say the Danes and Swedes rushed Olaf's line and were repulsed with heavy casualties and loss of ships. Eirik then forced his ship up against the last of Olaf's lashed-together ships and cleared it with a fierce attack, and so on, one ship after another, until only the Ormen Lange was left.

Around 975, Harold I of Denmark tried to force Christianity on the staunchly pagan Haakon Sigurdsson Jarl. Haakon broke his allegiance to Denmark, and a Danish invasion force was defeated at the battle of Hjörungavágr in 986.

Snorri Sturluson records that Harald Fairhair often used quickfire, house-burning, as an alternative to battles and alongside them. One of his first deeds was killing four petty kings, either by fire or with weapons, in a single quickfire raid. According to Snorri, this let him seize Hedemark, Ringerike, Gudbrandsdal, Hadeland, Thoten, Raumarike and the whole northern part of Vingulmark.

Scandinavians called Varangians, meaning "sworn men" in Old Norse, served the Byzantine emperors as bodyguards. This force was known as the Varangian Guard, and the Slavs and Byzantines used the name for Norse warriors more widely.

When the Ormen Lange was overpowered, Jarl Eirik captured the ship as Olaf threw himself into the sea. Danish sources report that Olaf killed himself, and Saxo Grammaticus says he jumped overboard in full armour rather than die at the enemy's hands or see his foes victorious. Norwegian and Icelandic accounts instead suggest he may have escaped to shore. Norway was afterwards ruled by the Jarls of Lade, who were allied as a suzerain to both the Danish Crown and the Commonwealth of Uppsala, Sweden.

Later accounts blame a family quarrel for the battle. Thyri, sister of Svein Forkbeard, married Olaf Tryggvason, but Svein refused to pay her promised dowry. Angered, Olaf set sail for the south with only 11 ships, expecting the rest to follow, but they did not.

The semi-legendary Swedish king Ingjald Illråde, who may have reigned in the 7th century, used quickfire at least twice to kill his opponents. First he burned several invited petty kings to death so he could rule their territories directly. Later he used it to kill Granmar, the last independent king of Södermanland.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that in 942 King Edmund I won a victory over the Norse kings of York. It quotes: "The Danes were previously subjected by force under the Norsemen, for a long time in bonds of captivity to the heathens." The Chronicle distinguishes the pagan Norwegian Norsemen of Dublin from the Christian Danes of the Danelaw.
Sources disagree on where Svolder was fought. Adam of Bremen places it in Øresund, while Icelandic sources place it near an island called Svolder, which is otherwise unknown.

In late 10th-century Iceland, thralls owned by Thorolf attempted a quickfire against the freedman Ulfar, his enemy. Thorolf's own son, Arnkel Goði, captured the thralls in the act and had them executed the following day. At Thorolf's request, Arnkel's rival Snorri Goði then prosecuted Arnkel for the unlawful killing of the thralls.

literature.text: The earliest written records from Scandinavia are runic inscriptions on memorial stones and other objects. Some contain allusions to Norse mythology and even short poems in alliterative verse.

Much Old Norse poetry was first preserved in oral culture, and the surviving body was mostly composed or written down in Iceland. Refined writing techniques such as vellum, pens and ink arrived seemingly at the same time as Christianity.

Old Norse poetry is conventionally split into Eddaic and Skaldic types. Eddaic poems treat mythology or ancient heroes in simpler meters with anonymous authors, while skaldic poetry praised living kings and nobles in more intricate meters by known poets called skalds.

The Younger Futhark reduced the older runic alphabet from 24 to 16 runes, a change complete by the late 8th century. It became the script of the Viking Age, and literacy in it became widespread, as shown by some 3,000 runestones, sometimes inscribed with almost casual notes.

Procopius's Thule is believed to describe part of Scandinavia, because several of its tribes are easily identified. They include the Geats (Gautoi) in present-day Sweden and the Sami people, whom he called the Scrithiphini.
The elaborate Rök runestone, dated to about 800, alludes to legends from the migration age. It is the best known example of runic inscriptions that carry poetry in alliterative verse.

The Icelanders' sagas usually take place from around the settlement of Iceland in the 870s to a generation or two after its conversion to Christianity in 1000. Stories from these times were passed on orally before being written down, though perhaps two thirds of the medieval corpus seem to date from the thirteenth century.

The reduction from the Elder to the Younger Futhark happened at the same time as phonetic changes, when Proto-Norse evolved into Old Norse. The main change was that the difference between voiced and unvoiced consonants was no longer expressed in writing. Writing also lost the spoken distinction between long and short vowels.
Procopius wrote that when the Herules returned, they passed the Warini and the Danes. They then crossed the sea to Thule, where they settled beside the Geats.

Poetry held a religious place in the Viking world. Even the oldest preserved poetry calls it 'the drink of the raven-god', meaning Odin, and Snorri Sturluson later recounted the myth of how Odin brought the mead of poetry to Asgard.

The tenth-century Arab Muslim writer Ahmad ibn Fadlan described a funeral near the Volga River of a chieftain of a people he called Rūsiyyah, whom scholars generally interpret as Scandinavian Rus'. A slave girl volunteered to die with him. She was given heavy drinks, had sex with the master of each tent, and was then pulled into the burial tent, where six men had intercourse with her while other men beat on their shields so her screams could not be heard. Two men pulled a rope looped around her neck while an old woman called the "Angel of Death" stabbed her between the ribs. The mourners also cut a dog in two and butchered two horses, two cows, a hen and a cock into the ship before setting it on fire.
The Younger Futhark is divided into long-branch (Danish) and short-twig (Swedish and Norwegian) runes. In the 10th century it was further expanded by the Hälsinge Runes, also called staveless runes.
Procopius says the inhabitants of Thule are pagans who practice human sacrifice. His Thule is believed to be the same place as Scandza, as described by Jordanes.
Around 122 verses are preserved in Swedish rune inscriptions, 54 in Norwegian ones and 12 in Danish ones. These stones show that poetry was carved as well as spoken.
Steinunn Refsdóttir, an Icelandic skald of the 10th century, is known for verses taunting the Christian missionary Þangbrandr.
Hildr Hrólfsdóttir, a Norwegian skald of around the 9th century, is known for her poetry about the banishment of her father Rolv Nevia. He was the Viking jarl of Trondheim.

The Younger Futhark became known in Europe as the alphabet of the Norsemen and was studied in the interest of trade and diplomatic contacts. It was called Abecedarium Nordmannicum in Frankish Fulda, possibly by Walahfrid Strabo.

science.text: The Gokstad ship had 16 rooms, meaning 32 oars, and a square sail of about 110 square metres. It is estimated that the sail could drive the ship at over 12 knots. The mast could be raised and lowered.

About 170 medieval swords carry the inscription +VLFBERH+T or +VLFBERHT+ on their blades. Most were found in Fennoscandia and around the Baltic Sea. They show a wide range of steels and production methods, such as a pattern welded core with welded-on hardened cutting edges.

Hedeby sat where a portage of less than 15 km linked the Schlei inlet to the Treene River, which flows into the Eider. Goods and ships were pulled overland on a corduroy road. This gave an almost uninterrupted seaway between the Baltic and the North Sea and avoided a dangerous circumnavigation of Jutland.

The Oseberg ship was 21.58 metres long and 5.10 metres broad, with 15 pairs of oar openings so that up to 30 people could row it. Its likely sail area of 90 square metres could have carried it at up to 10 knots. It also had a broad steering oar, an iron anchor and a bailer.

The runestones are unevenly distributed in Scandinavia. Sweden has between 1,700 and 2,500 depending on the definition, and the district of Uppland has the highest concentration with as many as 1,196 inscriptions in stone. Södermanland is second with 391.

Tree-ring dating, called dendrochronology, suggests the timber for the Gokstad ship was felled around 890 AD. That places its building at the end of the 9th century, during the reign of King Harald Fairhair.

The Gokstad ship's oak planks were tapered so each overlapped the plank above and below by about 30 mm, in clinker style. Iron rivets were set about 180 mm apart on straight stretches and about 125 mm apart where the planks turned.
Scientific dating suggests the Oseberg ship was buried no earlier than 834. Some parts of its structure date from as early as 800, and other parts may be even older.

In the 10th century, Frankish swordsmiths developed superior steels. Their swords had a higher carbon content, making them more durable, and were more manoeuvrable than Scandinavian-made swords. Local iron was useful, but the best swords and spearheads were undoubtedly imported.

Birka grave Bj 581 was long thought to hold a male warrior, and the skeleton was buried with a sword, an axe, a seax, spearheads, 25 arrowheads, two shield bosses and two bridled horses. A 2016 osteological analysis by Anna Kjellström and a 2017 DNA study led by Charlotte Hedenstierna-Jonson found the skeleton female, with two X chromosomes and no Y chromosome, and over the age of 30. The grave dates to the 10th century.
The Gokstad ship's oar holes could be hatched down when it was under sail. In shallow water, its rudder could be raised very quickly by undoing the fastening.

Fragments of the two women's skeletons from the Oseberg ship show how they lived. One, probably aged around 80, suffered badly from arthritis and had Morgagni's syndrome, which would have given her a masculine appearance and beard. The younger woman's teeth showed signs of a metal toothpick, a rare 9th century luxury, and her broken collarbone, first thought to be evidence of human sacrifice, had been healing for several weeks, though it is not clear whether one woman was sacrificed to accompany the other. Both women ate mainly meat, while most Vikings ate fish.

politics.text: Denmark was the first Scandinavian country to Christianize, when Harald Bluetooth declared it so around AD 965. He also raised the larger of the two Jelling Stones.

According to historian Anders Winroth, Christianity was not forced on Scandinavians by foreign states or missionaries. Scandinavian kings adopted it willingly, because they saw the religion as politically advantageous.

In 10th century Iceland, tension between Christian and pagan factions followed King Olaf I's taking of Icelandic hostages. Violent clashes were avoided when the Althing decided in 1000 AD to put the arbitration to Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði, leader of the pagan faction.
The earliest signs of Christianization in Scandinavia came in the 830s. Ansgar built churches in the trading towns of Birka and Hedeby.
The first known attempt to Christianize Sweden was made by Ansgar in 830, at the invitation of the Swedish king Björn. Ansgar set up a church at Birka but met with little Swedish interest.

Sweyn Forkbeard was king of Denmark from 986 and king of Norway from 1000; when he conquered England in 1013, he became the first king to unite all three kingdoms, beginning what historians call the North Sea Empire.
The Slavs and the Byzantines called the Norse Varangians, from Old Norse Væringjar, meaning 'sworn men'. The Scandinavian bodyguards of the Byzantine emperors were known as the Varangian Guard.

Sweden resisted conversion for a long time. Around a century after Ansgar, Unni, archbishop of Hamburg, made another unsuccessful attempt. In the 10th century, English missionaries did make inroads in Västergötland.

After Olaf's defeat at the Battle of Svolder in 1000, Norway partly returned to paganism under the rule of the Jarls of Lade. In the following reign of Saint Olaf, pagan remnants were stamped out and Christianity was entrenched.

At the Althing in 1000 AD, Þorgeir meditated for a day and a night before ruling that Iceland should convert to Christianity as a whole. Pagan worship in private would still be tolerated, which helped avoid violence between the two factions.

philosophy.text: Old Norse philosophy is best attested in the Poetic Edda, especially the Hávamál, a poem attributed to Odin. It taught that happiness could only be reached through a life of virtue. The key virtues were wisdom, self-control and personal independence.

The Norse cosmos consisted of Nine Worlds arranged around a central sacred tree, Yggdrasil. Units of time and elements of the cosmology were personified as deities or beings. This gave the Norse a structured picture of the universe told through myth.

Old Norse philosophy prized independence, self-reliance, loyalty, modesty, hospitality, generosity, compassion and courage, and above all wisdom. Independence meant more than material self-sufficiency, since it also meant independence of thought and action. Complete independence could only be reached through wisdom.

In one Norse creation myth, the world is created from the flesh of the primordial being Ymir. The first two humans are Ask and Embla, who according to the Prose Edda and the Poetic Edda poem Völuspá were driftwood found by a trio of gods and imbued with life in the form of three gifts. This story sits alongside the tale of the Nine Worlds around Yggdrasil.

Norse myth foretells that the worlds will be reborn after Ragnarök, an immense battle between the gods and their enemies in which the world is enveloped in flames. After the cataclysm, the world is reborn anew. The surviving gods meet on fertile, green land, and two humans, Líf and Lífþrasir, who survive in a wood, repopulate the world.

Til árs ok friðar, meaning "For a good year and peace", was an Old Norse ritual formula. It was used when drinking at blót-feasts and when making offerings at howes, in particular in association with Freyr. Its use is very similar in heathen and Christian contexts.

As in Aristotelian ethics, the Old Norse view held that wisdom could only be acquired through experience. An important source of that experience was traveling. The ultimate expression of independence was the ability to act in accordance with wisdom.

The author of the Hávamál points out that while wealth is temporary, wisdom is eternal. Wealth is dismissed as "the most fickle of friends". The poem thus ranks inner understanding above material possessions.

Scholars disagree about where Til árs ok friðar came from. Klaus Düwel suggested it came from missionary language, but Anders Hultgård found no Christian prototypes for it. Hultgård proposed that the medieval Church adopted it from the traditional religion as a form of syncretism during the Christianisation of Scandinavia.

Scholars such as Guðmundur Finnbogason and Sveinbjorn Johnson noted striking similarities between Old Norse philosophy and ancient Greek philosophy, in particular that of Homer and Aristotle. These similarities appear to result from independent development rather than outside influence.

culture.text: A prominent Viking Age burial tradition was the ship burial, in which the dead were laid in a boat or a stone ship. They were given grave offerings that matched their earthly status and profession, sometimes including sacrificed slaves. Piles of stone and soil were usually laid on top to create a barrow.

In 1000 AD, Christians and pagans in Iceland were kept from violent clashes when the Althing put the decision to Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði, the leader of the pagan faction. After a day and a night of meditation, he ruled that the whole country should convert to Christianity. Pagan worship in private would still be tolerated.

Norsemen and Slavs significantly intermixed, and the two cultures influenced each other. They were described as closely linked, fighting one another, intermixing and trading. Denmark was called a melting pot of Slavic and Scandinavian elements.

The most sumptuous Viking funeral discovered so far is the Oseberg Ship burial, made for a woman who lived in the 9th century. She was probably a queen or a priestess. Grave goods like hers not only symbolized status but also represented key moments or successes in a person's life.

What a person was buried with reflected who they were. A free man was usually given weapons and equipment for riding, while a blacksmith could receive his entire set of tools. Women were provided with their jewelry and often with tools for female and household activities.

The usual grave for a thrall was probably not much more than a hole in the ground. He was probably buried so that he could not return to haunt his masters, and so that he could be of use to them after they died. Slaves were sometimes sacrificed to be useful in the next life.
A grave of a warrior-woman dating to the 10th century in Denmark was long thought to belong to a Viking. New analyses revealed that she was a Slav from present-day Poland.

Jelling in Denmark is the largest royal memorial of the Viking Age. Harald Bluetooth made it in memory of his parents Gorm and Tyra, and in honour of himself. Its barrows, church and two Jelling stones show how important it was to mark death ritually in the pagan era and the earliest Christian times.

Til árs ok friðar, meaning "For a good year and peace", is an Old Norse ritual formula recorded with drinking at blót-feasts and with offerings made at howes. It is especially associated with Freyr. Scholars debate whether it began as a heathen or a Christian phrase.
